title: PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?
claim: A paper can be scored from text or page images by fine-tuned models, trained on anonymized corpora, and these models beat frontier systems.
layout: 3 panels: top pipeline left-to-right, bottom dataset diagram and result plots
description: The figure has three panels. Panel (a), across the top, is a left-to-right flow. A Paper icon splits into two branches: screenshots (layout and figures) feed PaperScorer-Vision, a blue box labeled fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and markdown text feeds PaperScorer-Text, a yellow box labeled fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B. Both branches merge into a Calibrated output box showing P_accept = 0.71 and a green Accept / red Reject bar. Panel (b), bottom left, shows two anonymized corpora. OpenReview connects to ICLR. arXiv expands into a grid of venue boxes (NeurIPS, CVPR, ICLR, etc.). Paper counts appear below each: 24,888 and 83,656. Panel (c), bottom right, has a grouped bar chart comparing PaperScorer-Vision and PaperScorer-Text with Gemini and GPT on ICLR and arXiv test sets, plus a line plot of accuracy against human rating percentile. The blue Vision model is highlighted as best.
caption: (a) PaperScorer is a family of models trained to predict a paper’s accept/reject decision from either a pure text or a visual view of the paper. (b) For training and evaluation, we built two fully anonymized datasets, sourced from OpenReview and arXiv and labeled with accept/reject decisions. (c) Across training recipes, we find fine-tuning on our large-scale corpora enables PaperScorer to exceed frontier models (GPT/Gemini), specifically on highly rated papers.
abstract: Automated research is largely evaluated by benchmark performance, but the value of research rarely reduces to a single score. Humans judge a work's holistic contribution through peer review, which is hard to model because it is noisy and depends on many factors. However, what if, given only the paper, we could predict its peer-review decision directly? We introduce PaperScorer, a family of models that predict a paper's accept or reject decision from its extracted text or page screenshots, training only on the decision after removing author identity and formatting shortcuts. Vision models are the most predictive (68% accuracy on ICLR papers and 77% on ML papers from arXiv), beating text-only and frontier reasoning models. Unlike plain text, page images retain figures, layout, and presentation. This signal is robust, surviving smaller models and even compressing the whole paper into a single image. But accurate predictions are not evenly spread. PaperScorer is strongest on the lowest and highest rated papers, while papers rated in the middle stay unpredictable for our models and frontier systems alike. Additionally, its confidence is calibrated, so its most confident predictions are also its most accurate. Overall, PaperScorer shows how much of the decision a paper carries on its own, marking a first step toward AI-driven research evaluation.
